content: Carbides are chemical compounds composed of carbon and a more electronegative element. They are of significant industrial importance. For instance, calcium carbide serves as a key feedstock in the chemical industry, while iron carbide (Fe₃C, also known as cementite) is formed in steel to enhance its properties. Carbides can be categorized based on their chemical bonding into the following types: 1. Salt-like ionic compounds. 2. Covalent compounds. 3. Interstitial compounds. 4. Intermediate transition metal carbides, which exhibit bonding characteristics between salt-like and interstitial carbides. Other specialized types of carbides include: Graphite intercalation compounds. Alkali metal fullerides. Endohedral fullerenes, where a metal atom is encapsulated within a fullerene molecule. Metallocarbohedrenes (met-cars), which are cluster compounds containing C₂ units. Examples of Carbides Calcium carbide (CaC₂): An industrially important ionic salt. Silicon carbide (SiC, carborundum): A covalent compound. Tungsten carbide (WC): An interstitial compound widely used in cutting tools. Cementite (iron carbide, Fe₃C): A critical component of steel. Boron carbide (B₄C): A very hard material with industrial applications. Tantalum carbide (TaC) and titanium carbide (TiC): Refractory materials with high hardness. Types of Carbides Ionic Carbides Salt-like carbides are formed by metals from: Group 1 (alkali metals). Group 2 (alkaline earth metals). Group 3 (scandium, yttrium, lanthanum). Group 11 (copper, silver, gold). Group 12 (zinc, cadmium, mercury). Aluminum from Group 13 (other Group 13 elements do not form carbides). Lanthanides and actinides, which form MC₂ and M₂C₃ carbides. Most ionic carbides are salts of the C₂²⁻ ion, also known as acetylides, ethynides, or acetylene diides. Some compounds contain other anionic species, such as: C⁴⁻ (methanides): These hydrolyze to produce methane gas. C₃⁴⁻ (sesquicarbides): These hydrolyze to yield methylacetylene. The naming of ionic carbides is inconsistent and can be confusing. Acetylides The C₂²⁻ ion contains a triple bond between the two carbon atoms. For example, in LaC₂, the bond length is 130.3 pm. The bonding in LaC₂ can be described as La³⁺ with an extra electron delocalized into the antibonding orbital of C₂²⁻, which explains its metallic conductivity. Methanides The monatomic ion C⁴⁻ is a very strong base and reacts with four protons to form methane (CH₄). Methanides, such as Be₂C and Al₄C₃, react with water to produce methane. For example: C⁴⁻ + 4H⁺ → CH₄ Some compounds, like Mg₂C₃, contain the C₃⁴⁻ ion, which hydrolyzes to form methylacetylene (CH₃C≡CH). Covalent Carbides Silicon and boron form covalent carbides. Silicon carbide (SiC) has two crystalline forms related to the diamond structure. Boron carbide (B₄C) has an unusual structure with icosahedral boron units linked by carbon atoms, similar to boron-rich borides. Both SiC and B₄C are extremely hard, refractory materials with significant industrial applications. Interstitial Carbides Carbides of Group 4, 5, and 6 transition metals (except chromium) are often described as interstitial compounds. These carbides are chemically inert, exhibit metallic properties, and are refractory. For example, titanium carbide (TiC) and tungsten carbide (WC) are widely used in industrial applications, such as coating metals for cutting tools. The structure of interstitial carbides involves carbon atoms fitting into octahedral interstices in a close-packed metal lattice. When the metal atoms are cubic close-packed (ccp), filling all octahedral interstices results in a 1:1 stoichiometry with a rock salt structure. When the metal atoms are hexagonal close-packed (hcp), filling only one set of interstices achieves a 2:1 stoichiometry with a CdI₂ structure. The packing of the metal lattice in carbides differs from that of the pure metal. Non-stoichiometric phases, once thought to be disordered, have been found to exhibit both shortand long-range ordering. Intermediate Transition Metal Carbides In these carbides, the transition metal ion is smaller than the critical 135 pm, resulting in more complex structures rather than interstitial arrangements. Multiple stoichiometries are common. For example, iron forms several carbides, including Fe₃C, Fe₇C₃, and Fe₂C. Cementite (Fe₃C) is the best-known example and is present in steels. These carbides are more reactive than interstitial carbides. For instance, the carbides of chromium, manganese, iron, cobalt, and nickel are hydrolyzed by dilute acids and sometimes by water, producing a mixture of hydrogen and hydrocarbons. These compounds share characteristics with both inert interstitial carbides and more reactive salt-like carbides.
